source_refs.note: Topic 29.5.1 with Example 29.1 (PDF 193); the printed spectra are not reproduced and are replaced by labelled schematic sketches. The printed 'cm' units are read as cm-1.

blocks.text: The best way to learn to interpret IR spectra is to study worked examples and become familiar with the characteristic features of a spectrum.

blocks.title: Example 29.1
blocks.text: Two spectra belong to propan-2-ol and propanone. A strong, sharp absorption at about 1710 cm-1 shows a C=O (carbonyl) group, the functional group of a ketone, so spectrum A is propanone. A strong absorption around 3200-3600 cm-1 in spectrum B shows an alcohol -OH group, so B is propan-2-ol.

blocks.alt: Three schematic IR spectra (not measured data) from 4000 to 500 cm-1 with dips for absorption. Propanone: a C-H dip near 2950 and a deep, sharp C=O dip near 1710 cm-1. Propan-2-ol: a broad, deep O-H dip centred near 3350 cm-1 and C-H near 2950, with no C=O dip. A carboxylic acid: a very broad O-H dip spanning about 2500-3300 cm-1 and a sharp C=O near 1700 cm-1.
blocks.caption: How the key bands look in a ketone, an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (original sketches, positions from Table 29.2).
blocks.long_description: Look first above 1500 cm-1. A sharp, strong dip near 1700 cm-1 means C=O; a broad dip at 3200-3600 cm-1 means an alcohol O-H; a very broad dip from 2500 to 3300 cm-1 together with C=O means a carboxylic acid. These sketches show only the shapes and positions, not real measured spectra.
